The controlling study defines its exposure by ICD-10 R49.0 (dysphonia, which includes aphonia) and is cross-sectional; if a qualified human finds longitudinal or treatment-discordant-cohort data separating communication-disability effects from reverse causation, the tier may be revisited.
governanceNotes: Authored conservatively at ASSOCIATION_ONLY strength: the large All of Us cross-sectional analysis found elevated odds of depression and anxiety in dysphonia (aOR 1.34 and 1.44) and voice-clinic cohorts show elevated psychological-distress caseness, but all evidence is cross-sectional, reverse causation is untested, and the exposure is broader than complete voice loss.

Severity-transparency guard recorded: the epidemiologic exposure (R49.0 dysphonia) spans hoarseness through complete voice loss, so the recorded associations cannot be assumed to scale to aphonia severity; individual determination belongs entirely to examination findings and a qualified medical professional.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: The All of Us cross-sectional analysis of 283,137 adults, whose exposure was the ICD-10 dysphonia code R49.0 encompassing aphonia, found 1.34 times the adjusted odds of depression (95% CI 1.27-1.41) in dysphonia after controlling for demographics, smoking, alcohol, and comorbidities (Weinstein 2026); a prospective voice-clinic cohort found 17% HADS caseness for anxiety and/or depression with strong emotional-VoiSS/HADS correlation, and noted organic laryngeal disorders carried more distress than functional dysphonia (Montgomery 2016); the retrospective voice-clinic cohort found 31.2% of voice-disorder patients with elevated depression scores, varying by diagnosis (Dietrich 2008).
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established at the mapping level: all three sources are cross-sectional or retrospective, depressive illness can itself alter voice use and care-seeking, the exposure code spans hoarseness to complete loss, and no longitudinal or treatment-discordant cohort separates disability effects from reverse causation, so no directional claim is made here.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: A communication-disability pathway is hypothesized: loss of voiced communication degrades identity, social participation, and occupational voice function, and the resulting isolation, frustration, and loss of agency feed the depressive cascade; shared neural links between laryngeal control and affect regulation are also proposed. The pathway is plausible and the co-occurrence is documented at scale, but the epidemiology is cross-sectional and reverse causation is untested, so no directional claim is made here.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: This relationship is supported as an association only. Voice-disorder populations show elevated depression prevalence across large epidemiologic and clinic-cohort data; individual determination requires psychiatric diagnostic documentation of the depressive episode with chronology relative to the voice loss, exclusion of premorbid and independent depression, and review by a qualified medical professional.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: Structured psychiatric evaluation documenting the depressive episode (duration, severity, functional impact) with chronology relative to voice-loss onset; ENT documentation of the voice disorder (laryngoscopy findings, etiology, treatment history); exclusion of premorbid depression, substance use, and independent psychosocial stressors of equal potency; occupational and social-participation impact documentation; a medical professional's opinion connecting the documented findings in this individual case
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Premorbid or independent depressive disorder preceding the voice loss
Shared drivers (smoking, head-and-neck disease, chronic illness burden) depressing mood directly
Reactive adjustment naturally resolving without depressive-disorder threshold
Functional (psychogenic) voice loss as a manifestation of the psychiatric condition itself (reverse direction)
Medication effects (e.g., inhaled corticosteroid dysphonia populations with comorbid disease)

suggestions.rationale: Authored conservatively at association-only strength: the co-occurrence is documented at scale in the largest available dataset, but cross-sectional design defeats directional claims and the exposure is broader than aphonia; the edge records documented co-occurrence only.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: The All of Us cross-sectional analysis found 1.44 times the adjusted odds of anxiety (95% CI 1.37-1.52) in ICD-10 R49.0 dysphonia, the largest psychiatric association in that dataset (Weinstein 2026); the voice-clinic cohort found 20% borderline and 17% positive HADS anxiety and/or depression caseness with the emotional VoiSS subscale tracking anxiety at Spearman's rho 0.68 (Montgomery 2016); the retrospective voice-clinic cohort found 36.9% of patients with elevated anxiety scores, the most frequent elevation among the measured domains and highest in paradoxical vocal fold movement disorder (Dietrich 2008).
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established at the mapping level: all evidence is cross-sectional or retrospective, anxiety states can themselves produce or amplify voice symptoms (including paradoxical vocal fold motion), and the exposure spans hoarseness to complete loss, so no directional claim is made here.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: A communication-threat pathway is hypothesized: inability to produce voice creates anticipatory anxiety about communication failures, social evaluation, and occupational consequences, with hypervigilance to vocal symptoms maintaining the anxiety cycle; the same psychosocial disability substrate proposed for depression underlies the anxiety association. The pathway is plausible and co-occurrence is documented at scale, but the epidemiology is cross-sectional and reverse causation is untested, so no directional claim is made here.
